blocks: Mixer specs give maximum input and output levels in dBu, and noise as a negative dBu figure. See Audio/Signal Level.
A direct injection box: it takes an instrument's unbalanced, high-impedance signal and turns it into a Audio/Balanced, low-impedance, mic-level signal on an Audio/Connector/XLR.
It lets a guitar, bass or keyboard plug into a mic input on a long cable. Its input gives the pickup the same light load as a Audio/Hi-Z input.
Passive DIs use a transformer and need no power. Active DIs use electronics powered by a battery or by Audio/Phantom Power.
A ground-lift switch on most DIs breaks a hum loop between the instrument and the mixer.
Short for equalizer: raising or lowering the level of a range of frequencies to change a sound's tone.
Shelving bands lift or cut everything above or below a frequency. A mixer's LOW and HIGH knobs are usually shelves.
Peaking bands lift or cut a range around a centre frequency. A MID knob is one.

A small mixer's channel EQ has fixed frequencies, so each knob sets only the amount, often ±15 dB. A software EQ such as Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/16 EQ Three or Ableton/Live/UG/29 Audio Effect Reference/15 EQ Eight lets you move the frequencies as well.
The noise of a Audio/Mic Preamp at its input. It is measured at full gain and divided by the gain, so preamps with different gain ranges can be compared.
Given in Audio/dBu, or as a positive dB figure that means the same thing. More negative is quieter.

Compare EIN only between figures measured the same way. A lower source impedance, a narrower bandwidth or A-weighting makes the number look better, so a 50 Ω figure looks a few dB quieter than a 150 Ω one.
A high-impedance input, around 1 MΩ, built for passive guitar and bass pickups. Labels also read INST or GUITAR.
A passive pickup sounds dull and quiet on a normal line input, whose 10–20 kΩ loads it down. The high impedance leaves the pickup's treble intact.
Without a Hi-Z input, a Audio/DI Box does the same job in front of a mic input. See Audio/Signal Level.
The amplifier at the front of a mic input that raises the mic's signal to line level, so the rest of the mixer can work with it. Its GAIN knob sets how much.
A mic delivers a signal tens of dB below line level (Audio/Signal Level), so the preamp needs up to 60 dB of gain or more. Its own noise at that gain is measured as Audio/EIN.
Too much gain clips the preamp, which a CLIP LED shows. Too little leaves the signal close to the noise floor.
Mixer channels with a mic preamp usually also offer Audio/Phantom Power.
DC power a mixer or recorder sends up a mic cable to power a condenser mic. The cable carries the audio and the power together, on the same pins of an Audio/Connector/XLR.

The standard is +48 V, labelled P48. The voltage sits equally on pins 2 and 3, so the Audio/Balanced input that reads the difference between them doesn't hear it. Some gear also offers +12 V and +24 V, as the Zoom H5/UG/13 Settings/03 Phantom Power does.
Dynamic mics and balanced line sources ignore it. Turn it off before plugging in a ribbon mic or an unbalanced source, or when patching with the channel up, to avoid damage and loud pops.
Mixers often switch it for a group of inputs at once, as on the Behringer/Mixer/XENYX 802S.
The rough voltage range an audio output delivers, which sets the kind of input it needs. An input built for one level clips or sounds too quiet with another.
Mic level — tens of dB below line level, needing a Audio/Mic Preamp.
Instrument level — a passive guitar or bass pickup, below line level and from a high-impedance source, needing a Audio/Hi-Z input or a Audio/DI Box.
Line level — +4 dBu for pro gear, −10 dBV for consumer gear (Audio/dBu). Synths, interfaces and mixer outputs work at line level.
Speaker level — the output of a power amplifier, many volts, for passive speakers only.

Machine-to-Machine (M2M) authentication covers server-to-server and service-to-service communication flows where no human user is present to authorize the request
Typically implemented via the OAuth2 Client Credentials flow (RFC 6749 §4.4)
The client presents its client_id and client_secret directly to the authorization server and receives a short-lived access token — usually a JWT
No user redirect or consent screen; the token represents the service itself, not a delegated user

An Amazon EC2 feature for carving isolated execution environments, called enclaves, out of an EC2 instance. An enclave is a hardened, highly constrained virtual machine with no persistent storage, no interactive access (no SSH), and no external networking. Its only link to the parent instance is a local socket.
Processes and users on the parent instance, root included, cannot read the enclave's memory or data. The AWS Nitro Hypervisor isolates the enclave's vCPUs and memory from the parent.
Supports cryptographic attestation, so a service can verify which code is running in an enclave. AWS/KMS key policies can require that an enclave's measurements match before a key operation succeeds.
Meant for sensitive data such as PII and the applications that process it.

Limits: up to four enclaves per parent instance, enclaves cannot talk to each other, enclaves stop when the parent stops, no hibernation on the same instance. The enclave must run Linux. The parent runs Linux or Windows on most Intel, AMD, and Graviton instance types built on the Nitro System.
No extra charge beyond the EC2 instance and other AWS services used.

Typical use: Steady or slowly scaled HTTP services, internal APIs, prototypes that graduate to always‑on endpoints, teams wanting ECS/Fargate outcomes without assembling every piece manually first.
Shared ground: Both often involve containers on AWS and elastic capacity; both can appear in architectures that serve AI products (e.g. an API fronting a model).

Different core job: Express Mode optimizes service deployment and operations for durable endpoints (routing, scaling policies, hosted URLs). E2B optimizes mass ephemeral sandboxes for agent code execution, notebooks, browsers/desktops for agents, etc., with productized lifecycle and templates. You might run both (Express Mode for your control plane API; E2B or self‑managed sandboxes for per‑task isolation), but they are not substitutes for the same problem.

Relation to AWS/Lightsail: Express Mode is ECS/Fargate‑native and container‑first; Lightsail is VM/bundle‑first. Express Mode targets production ECS patterns; Lightsail targets simplicity of a small fleet of instances and add‑ons.
